newsitem.title: USA: Strong exports boost grain prices, gold ends lower.
newsitem.headline: Strong exports boost grain prices, gold ends lower.

text.p: Strong export demand pushed up grain and soybean prices on Thursday and gold prices eased as details of a shocking revision to a Canadian company's Indonesian gold find continued to come to light.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean meal and wheat led the charge higher as a weekly report from the Agriculture Department showed stronger than expected export shipments.
Soybean meal for May delivery closed $6 a ton higher at $282.70 and May soybeans closed up 14 cents a bushel at $8.55.

Traders said soymeal exports of 209,800 metric tons exceeded expectations of only 80,000 to 150,000 tons, while soybean shipments of 387,000 tons were also better than expected given strong competition from new-crop soybeans now being harvested in Brazil, the major U.S. rival for exports.
"Beans were up with meal on the export sales," said analyst Jack Scoville of brokerage LIT America.
"Demand has been good enough that the U.S. markets have been very competitive with the South American markets, which is incredibly unusual for this time of year," he said.
The spillover from soybeans aided grain prices, with May corn closing up 3 cents a bushel at $3.08-1/4 and May wheat up 6-1/4 cents a bushel at $4.01-3/4.
Weekly corn exports of 569,000 tons were as most expected, but wheat exports of 497,000 tons were well above most trade guesses of 100,000 to 300,000 tons.

Suspicions that India may need to buy large amounts of wheat were fed by an announcement from India's Civil Supplies Ministry that foodgrain stocks on December 1 fell to 20.36 million tons from 29.89 million a year earlier.
Export traders said India bought 1 million tons of Australian wheat this week and might buy another 500,000 tons soon. The Australian Wheat Board declined comment on the market talk on Thursday.

At the Commodity Exchange in New York, gold prices closed lower ahead of the long Easter weekend holiday, failing to draw much strength from weakness in stocks and the dollar and mostly shrugging off Bre-X Mineral's Indonesian gold woes.
"Monday is first notice day in the gold and we had some book-squaring ahead of that. The rollover and spread trading accounted for the bulk of activity," Tim Porter of Refco said.
Gold for June delivery ended $1.00 lower at $352.50 an ounce, ending the week comfortably above the key psychological level of $350.00 an ounce.

Gold traders said the surprising news that gold deposits at at Calgary-based Bre-X Minerals' gold property at Busang, Indonesia, may have been vastly overestimated had battered shares of gold mining companies much more than it had affected bullion prices.

"The XAU (Philadelphia gold shares index) is being murdered" by the fallout from Bre-X, said Greg Drury of Mitsui and Co USA. "But on the actual gold spot price, I don't think Bre-X is making any difference at all."
The XAU index closed down 5.09 points at 105.10.
The Busang deposit had been considered "the find of the century" as recently as last month, when a Bre-X official estimated it held up to 200 million ounces of gold.
But Bre-X Chief Executive David Walsh admitted Wednesday such claims were likely overstated due to "invalid samples and assaying of those samples."
Bre-X shares plunged $13 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Thursday to $2.50 (Canadian), wiping out $3 billion in market value from the company.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for May delivery closed up 2.95 cents a pound at 189.80 cents.
The contract rose 24 cents or 14 percent on the week as worries about this year's supplies returned to the market and sparked buying by roasters and speculators.
The Association of Coffee Producing Countries on Thursday cut its estimates for Central American coffee production this year by 400,000 132-pound bags.
It also said coffee available to world roasters in the third quarter of this year would be smaller than last year at 17.91 million bags.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed mixed in quiet trade. May crude oil ended 6 cents a barrel higher at $20.70, April gasoline fell 0.19 cent a gallon to 64.63 cents, and April heating oil rose 0.64 cent a gallon to close at 56.07 cents.
